inline.s: [Q: The "ten recitations" of the Larger Sutra and the "single recitation" of the jewel-king treatise — do these belong to ordinary times or to the moment of death? A: The "ten recitations" span both times. The "morning ten recitations" belong to ordinary times; the "ten recitations that bring rebirth," like the ten recitations of the name described in the Contemplation Sutra, belong to the moment of death. The "single recitation," however, refers only to the moment of death.]

A student asked: The Larger Sutra speaks of "attaining rebirth through ten recitations," and the Jewel-King Treatise speaks of "attaining rebirth through a single recitation." Do these ten recitations and that single recitation refer to ordinary times or to the moment of death? Master Ouyi replied: Generally, the "ten recitations" have two senses — one refers to ordinary times, the other to the moment of death. The "morning ten recitations" advocated by the Repentance Master Ciyun refer to ordinary times; "attaining rebirth through ten recitations," being the same as the "ten recitations of the name" in the Contemplation Sutra, refers to the final ten recitations at the moment of death. And the "attaining rebirth through a single recitation" spoken of in the Jewel-King Treatise refers only to the single final recitation at the moment of death.

[The "ten recitations" of the Larger Sutra] refers to the "attaining rebirth through ten recitations" spoken of in the Sutra of Immeasurable Life. [The "single recitation" of the Jewel-King] refers to the "attaining rebirth through a single recitation" in the ninth section, "The Gate of Single Recitation and Ten Recitations in This Life and the Next," of the Treatise on the Jewel-King Samādhi of Buddha-Recitation.

[Q: If both ten recitations and a single recitation bring rebirth, why should there be need of the seven days of practice? A: Were there no ordinary, daily practice of seven days, how could there be the ten or the single recitations at the moment of death? Even those of the lowest grade who have committed the worst offenses — all are cases where the karmic causes of past lives have matured, so that at death they meet a good spiritual friend, and upon hearing they give rise to faith and vows. Such a matter occurs in not one case out of ten thousand — how can one presume upon good fortune! The Questions on the Pure Land refutes this most thoroughly, and people of today must read it.]

The student further asked: Whether it is ten recitations or a single recitation, both can bring rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss; then why should there be any need of reaching the practice of single-minded, undisturbed concentration? Master Ouyi replied: Were there no daily, single-minded undisturbed practice, where could the ten or the single recitations at the moment of death come from? Even those of the lowest grade who have committed the rebellious and evil deeds — all are cases where the karmic causes of past lives have matured, so that at the moment of death they encounter a good spiritual friend and, upon hearing, give rise to faith and vows. Such a matter occurs in not one case out of ten thousand — how can one presume upon good fortune! The Questions on the Pure Land refutes this fallacious view that "since both ten recitations and a single recitation bring rebirth, why need there be single-minded concentration in ordinary times" in the greatest detail, and people of today must read it.

As for the question of the ten recitations at the moment of death, Master Ouyi, in the "Preface to a Repentance and Life-Release Society of the Lingfeng Collected Works," discussed: The ten recitations at the moment of death require that roots of goodness be deeply planted, so that at death right mindfulness can appear. If now, when conditions of adversity or advantage arise, there is no longer right mindfulness, how much less can one maintain right mindfulness at the moment of death? Moreover, now, in broad daylight, in the clear and open, one cannot yet faithfully accept and practice the true exhortations of an illumined teacher or good friend; and yet one hopes that when the suffering of death appears, one can, merely by relying on a good friend's reminder and instruction, accomplish this faithful acceptance and practice? Even more, at the moment of death, how can one be sure that a true good friend will appear? Even if a genuine good friend does appear, if at the time of that instruction the person's consciousness is clouded and bewildered, then to seek one's faith and understanding — this is again a completely impossible matter! (The original text reads: "The ten recitations at death must have deeply planted roots of goodness. Now when adverse and favorable conditions arise, there is no longer right mindfulness, how much less at death? Moreover, when the suffering of death appears, one merely relies on a good friend to correct and awaken one; now, in broad daylight, one still cannot faithfully accept and practice the true maxims of an illumined teacher and friend! At the moment of death, how can one secure the appearance of a good friend? Suppose he appears and teaches, but the consciousness is clouded, and one seeks faith and understanding of it — this again is an impossibility.")

From this one understands that "attaining rebirth through ten recitations" means the final ten recitations at the moment of death, and "attaining rebirth through a single recitation" likewise means the final single recitation at the moment of death — it is the final resolution at the moment of death that is the true resolution. At the moment of death it is like a person arriving at the airport: ordinarily one speaks of going here or going there, but where one actually ends up depends entirely on which plane one finally boards. Therefore, being able to concentrate single-mindedly on one recitation of the Buddha's name, or ten recitations, at the final moment of death is of crucial importance.

As for the relationship between attaining rebirth through ten or a single recitation and single-minded undisturbed concentration, Master Ouyi clearly states: "Were there no ordinary, daily practice of seven days (the single-minded undisturbed practice of ordinary times), how could there be the ten or the single recitations at the moment of death?"

As for the state of mind of the person who has committed the five rebellious offenses and the ten evil acts and, at the moment of death, is reborn through ten recitations, Master Yinguang instructed: Though he has not personally realized single-minded undisturbed concentration, still his mind at the moment of death, apart from the thought of reciting the Buddha, has in the end no other thought. (The original words of Master Yinguang: "The Contemplation Sutra speaks of the five rebellious offenses and ten evil acts: as one is about to die, the signs of hell appear; a good spiritual friend (the original note: this is not restricted to monastics or lay, whether man or woman — whoever can teach him to recite the Buddha is called a good spiritual friend) teaches him to recite the Buddha; perhaps only ten sounds, perhaps fewer than ten, and then death comes — he too relies on the Buddha's compassionate power and is reborn while still bearing karma. These ten recitations, compared with ordinary ten recitations, have the force of a vast gulf — their ferocity and urgency differ utterly — and so birth is attained. Driven by the utmost suffering of hell, as soon as he hears the Buddha's name he invokes it with his whole spirit; apart from this thought there is absolutely no other thought. Though he has not personally realized single-minded undisturbed concentration, still his mind in the end is without any other thought." (Collected Writings of Master Yinguang, Third Collection, Volume Two, "Letter in Reply to Layman Chen Xinru"))
Master Chewu, in his Posthumous Collection, says:

[Our present single thought is conditionally arising yet without inherent nature; without inherent nature it is yet conditionally arising. If it does not arise in the Buddha realm, it arises in the nine realms. From the standpoint of conditional arising and the absence of inherent nature, all beings and the Buddha are equal — both one emptiness. From the standpoint of the absence of inherent nature yet conditional arising, the ten realms differ immensely in excellence and inferiority. When King Ajita was at the point of death, because the man swatting flies carelessly brushed his face with a fan, a single thought of anger arose, and through this single thought of anger at death he fell into a poisonous snake. A woman, crossing a river, lost her grip, and her child fell into the water; because she tried to save the child, she too was submerged. Because her last thought was one of compassion, she was reborn in the heavens. When a single thought of compassion or anger at death thus divides heaven from the animal realm, can one afford to be careless about this single, conditionally arising thought at the moment of death? If at death one turns this mind to recollecting Amitābha Buddha and seeking rebirth in the Pure Land, how could one fail to see the Buddha and be reborn?]

Our present single thought is conditionally arising and without inherent nature; without inherent nature, it is yet conditionally arising. If it does not arise in the Buddha realm, it arises in the nine realms. From the standpoint of conditional arising and the absence of inherent nature, all beings and the Buddha are equal — both one emptiness. From the standpoint of the absence of inherent nature yet conditional arising, the ten realms differ immensely in excellence and inferiority. When King Ajita was at the point of death, because the fly-swatting man carelessly brushed his face with a fan, a single thought of anger arose; since this last thought at death was one of anger, he fell into a poisonous serpent. A woman, crossing a river, lost her grip, and her child fell into the water; because she went to save her child, she too was submerged. Because her last thought at death was one of compassion, the woman was reborn in the heavens. Thus, when the last thought is compassion or anger, the compassionate is reborn in heaven and the angry in the animal realm — their excellence and inferiority are thereby divided. Can one afford to be careless about this single, conditionally arising thought at the moment of death? If at death one uses this mind to recollect Amitābha Buddha and seek rebirth in the Pure Land, how could one fail to see the Buddha and be reborn?

[Without inherent nature] the teaching that "all dharmas have no inherent nature" means that no dharma has a real, solid entity; all are illusory appearances, like things in a dream. "Without inherent nature" is also called "without nature." The Treatise on Consciousness-Only says: "All dharmas are without inherent nature." The Lotus Sutra says: "Know that all dharmas are always without nature." The Śūraṅgama Sutra says: "All illusions become without nature." [King Ajita] — King Ajita, who in his life built countless Buddha-stupas, made offerings to the Three Jewels, protected the true Dharma, and had vast merit. At the point of death, because his attendant carelessly brushed his face with a fan, he gave rise to anger and fell into a venomous snake. The matter is found in the Miscellaneous Analogies Sutra.

[But this single thought cannot be obtained by relying on good fortune. One must hold it in sincerity and maintain it by constant practice. Therefore, with this single phrase "Amitābha Buddha," reciting it a thousand times, ten thousand times, up to the whole day and the whole year — this is all simply to ripen this single thought of recitation. If once this single thought is fully ripened, then at the moment of death there is only this single thought, no other. The Great Master Zhiyi says: "The mind fixed in samādhi at the moment of death is the very mind that receives rebirth in the Pure Land." Now if there is only this single thought with no other, is this not the mind fixed in samādhi? If the recitation is truly like this, and one does not see Amitābha, whom else will one see? If one is not reborn in the Pure Land, where else will one be reborn? I only fear that we ourselves cannot truly believe — that is all.]

But this single thought at the moment of death cannot be obtained by counting on good fortune. One must hold it in sincerity and maintain it by constant practice. Therefore, with this single phrase "Amitābha Buddha," reciting it a thousand times, ten thousand times, up to the whole day and the whole year, is nothing but ripening this single thought of recitation, so as to ensure that the thought at death is a thought of reciting Amitābha Buddha. If in truth the single thought of recitation is fully ripened, then at the moment of death there is only this single thought of recitation, and no other thought. The Great Master Zhiyi says: "The mind fixed in samādhi at the moment of death is the very mind that receives rebirth in the Pure Land." Now if there is only the thought of recitation and nothing else, is this not the mind fixed in samādhi? Since at the moment of death the mind is fixed in samādhi, if one does not see Amitābha Buddha, whom else will one see? If one is not reborn in the Pure Land, where else would one be reborn? I only fear that we ourselves cannot truly believe the above principle. If we truly believed, how could we not strive to ripen this single thought of recitation and be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss?

[To ripen this single thought] means to accomplish what Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta calls "pure thoughts continuing one after another," which is also what Master Shandao (the second Pure Land patriarch) calls "thought after thought unbroken." (Please note: "thought after thought unbroken" means that the thoughts of recitation continue unbroken from one to the next, and not the case of one's mouth continually reciting while the mind is given over to deluded imaginings.) Master Shandao says: "Therefore the Great Sage (Śākyamuni Buddha), out of compassion, directly urges us to single-mindedly invoke the Name. It is precisely because invoking the Name is easy that, with continuity, rebirth follows. If one can be unbroken thought after thought, taking the exhaustion of this life as the limit, then of ten, ten are reborn; of a hundred, a hundred. I pray that all people reflect well: whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying, one must spur the mind, restrain oneself, day and night never ceasing; when the former thought ends, the next thought is born, forever enjoying the bliss of the unconditioned, even up to Buddhahood — is this not joy! (Quoted from the Essentials of Buddha-Recitation.) Therefore, continuity of thought in ordinary times is the guarantee of right mindfulness at death; and right mindfulness at death is the key to rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Collected Writings of Master Yinguang, Third Collection
Volume Two
Letter in Reply to Layman Chen Xinru,' says:
[The Contemplation Sutra speaks of the five rebellious offenses and ten evil acts: as one is about to die, the signs of hell appear; a good spiritual friend
(the original note: this is not restricted to monastics or lay, whether man or woman — whoever can teach him to recite the Buddha is called a good spiritual friend)

teaches him to recite the Buddha; perhaps only ten sounds, perhaps fewer than ten, and then death comes — he too, relying on the Buddha's compassionate power, is reborn while still bearing karma. These ten recitations, compared with ordinary ten recitations, have the force of a vast gulf — their ferocity and urgency differ utterly — and so birth is attained. Driven by the utmost suffering of hell, as soon as he hears the Buddha's name he invokes it with his whole spirit; apart from this thought there is absolutely no other thought. Though he has not personally realized single-minded undisturbed concentration, still his mind in the end is without any other thought.]

The Contemplation Sutra of Immeasurable Life says that a person who has committed the five rebellious offenses and the ten evil acts, at the moment of death, when the signs of hell appear, is taught to recite the Buddha; though he recites only ten sounds, or not even ten before his breath ceases, he too, relying on the Buddha's compassionate power, is reborn while bearing karma. This is because these ten recitations, compared with ordinary ten recitations, have the force of a vast gulf — their fierceness and earnestness differ utterly — and so rebirth is attained. Driven by the utmost suffering of hell, as soon as he learns that reciting the Buddha can keep him from hell and bring rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, he invokes it with his whole spirit. Apart from this thought of recitation, there is absolutely no other thought. Though he has not personally realized single-minded undisturbed concentration, still at the moment of death his mind, apart from the thought of reciting the Buddha, is wholly without any other thought.

[The five rebellious offenses] are five kinds of extreme crimes against principle: killing one's father, killing one's mother, killing an arhat, drawing blood from the Buddha, and causing division in the Sangha. Because these are acts of extreme evil, the commission of any one of them leads to the Uninterrupted Hell. [The ten evil acts] are: killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, idle talk, harsh speech, divisive speech, greed, anger, and foolishness.
Collected Writings of Master Yinguang
Preface to the Beginner's Guide to the Pure Land Practice says:

[The minds of living beings are like water; Amitābha Buddha is like the moon. When living beings are complete in faith and vows and, with utmost sincerity, move the Buddha, the Buddha responds — just as when the water is clear, the moon appears. If the mind is not pure, not sincere, and accords with greed, anger, and delusion, it runs counter to the Buddha; like turbid, agitated water, though the moon does not withdraw its shining, it cannot be clearly reflected.]

The minds of living beings are like water; Amitābha Buddha is like the moon. When living beings are complete in faith and vows and, with utmost sincerity, move the Buddha to respond, the Buddha responds — just as when the water is clear, the moon appears. If the mind is impure and insincere, and accords with greed, anger, and delusion, then it runs counter to the Buddha; like turbid and agitated water, though the moon still shines upon it, it cannot be clearly reflected.

blocks.text: 6. The Teaching of Chan Master Yuanxian

inline.s: [Chan Master Yuanxian] was a monk of the Caodong school in the Ming dynasty (1578–1657), a native of Jianyang in Fujian, his lay surname Cai, his style name Yongjue. Born on the nineteenth day of the seventh month of the sixth year of the Wanli reign. Naturally gifted, he studied Confucian learning in his youth with considerable diligence and was accepted among the students of the district school. In the thirtieth year of Wanli (1602), at the age of twenty-five, he first learned that beyond Zhou and Confucius there was also the study of the Buddha and the Way, and so he steeped himself widely in the sutras and treatises, deeply probing their principle. The following year he took refuge under Shouchang Huijing, and at the age of forty received the tonsure from him. In the forty-sixth year of Wanli (1618), when Shouchang passed away, he served his disciple Boshan Yuanlai, receiving the full precepts, and then went to study at Xianglu Peak, Jinxian Hermitage, and Heshan for several years. In the ninth month of the third year of the Tianqi reign (1623), he returned to Fujian; passing through Jianjin on the way, he heard a man on a boat reciting the Lotus Sutra and at once had a great opening of mind. In the sixth year of the Chongzhen reign (1633), he received the Yunqi precepts from Wengu Guangyin; the next year he dwelt at Mount Gushan in Fuzhou, and subsequently at Kaiyuan Temple in Quanzhou, Zhenji Temple in Hangzhou, Baoshan Temple in Yanzhou, and other monasteries. Later he returned to Mount Gushan, renovating the monasteries and halls, and greatly revived the style of the Dong lineage; the people of the time all called him an Ancient Buddha come again. The Master's mind was set on the West, and he constantly urged people to cultivate the Pure Land karma. He passed away on the seventh day of the tenth month in the fourteenth year of the Shunzhi reign of the Qing, at the age of eighty. His disciples included Youlin Daopei and many others. He authored the thirty-fascicle Extensive Record of the Venerable Yongjue Xian, the ten-fascicle Brief Commentary on the Śūraṅgama Sutra, the one-fascicle Brief Commentary on the Diamond Sutra, the one-fascicle Pointing the Palm of the Heart Sutra of Prajñā, the four-fascicle Essentials of the Four-Part Vinaya, the three-fascicle Guide to the Study of the Vinaya, the one-fascicle Essential Words on Pure Wisdom, the four-fascicle Textual Study of the Sayings of the Chan School, the six-fascicle Continued Transmission of the Lamp, the two-fascicle Record of the Hongshi of Jianzhou, the two-fascicle Inner Collection of Chan Recreations, and the eight-fascicle Outer Collection of Chan Recreations.

[Chan Master Yongjue Yuanxian says: Though the work of the Pure Land karma is accumulated in ordinary times, the single final thought at the moment of death is of the utmost importance. For it is by this single thought that one is reborn in a pure land or a defiled land, and that one enters the sage's path or the path of the ordinary.]

Chan Master Yongjue Yuanxian instructed: Though the work of the Pure Land karma is accumulated in ordinary times, the single final thought at the moment of death is the most crucial. This is because whether one is reborn in a pure land or a defiled land, whether one enters the sage's stream or the ordinary position, is entirely determined by this single final thought at the moment of death!

[I often see those who recite the Buddha: in ordinary times they all say they seek rebirth in the Pure Land, but at the moment of death most have no right mindfulness. Either they cling to life and fear death, attached to this skin-bag; or their gaze turns to wife and children, unable to bear the parting; or their thoughts are tied to family wealth, unable to let it go; or, because circumstances run contrary to their wishes, they die nursing resentment; or, driven by the pressure of illness and pain, they depart swallowing their suffering. Having lost right mindfulness, they can but follow this unwholesome final thought and sink and fall.]

I often see those who recite the Buddha: ordinarily they all say they seek rebirth in the Pure Land, but when the moment of death comes, most of them have no right mindfulness. Either they are greedy for life and fear death, fond of this body; or their eyes turn toward wife and children, finding it hard to part; or their minds are tied to family possessions, unable to lay them down; or, because circumstances do not go as they wish, they die harboring resentment; or, pressed by the torment of illness, they depart swallowing pain. Having lost right mindfulness, they can but follow this unwholesome, non-right final thought at death and sink and fall into ruin.

[I urge cultivators to reach this point: simply believe the scriptures with true understanding, solidify right mindfulness, lay everything down, and recite the Buddha while awaiting the end. Alas! The matter of death is momentous, and in an instant the next life comes. A single thought made in error brings suffering through countless eons — how can one not fear!]

I urge cultivators, when the moment of death arrives, simply to believe the scriptures with true understanding, to solidify right mindfulness, to put everything down, and to go on reciting the Buddha without interruption until the breath stops. Alas! Birth and death are a great matter; in the twinkling of an eye comes the next life. If the final thought at death is a mistaken one, and it brings suffering through countless eons — how can one not be fearful!
(The original text is recorded from The Path Within the Path, the Meaning Expanded.)
Appendix
1. Whether rebirth is attained
2. The wonderful method of reciting the Buddha
3. A couplet for the Buddha-recitation hall
1. Whether rebirth is attained

Question: Please explain the meaning of "Whether rebirth is attained depends entirely on the presence or absence of faith and vows; the higher or lower grade depends entirely on the depth or shallowness of holding the name."

Answer: These two lines come from Master Ouyi's Essential Explanation of the Buddha-Spoken Amitābha Sutra, in its section on genuine faith and sincere vows, which says: "Faith, vows, and holding the name — these are the essential purport of the sutra. Faith and vows are the practice of wisdom; holding the name is the practice of action. Whether rebirth is attained depends entirely on the presence or absence of faith and vows; the higher or lower grade depends entirely on the depth or shallowness of holding the name. Hence the practice of wisdom is the guide, and the practice of action is the primary cultivation, like the eye and the foot working together."

In this passage, "faith, vows, and holding the name — the essential purport of the sutra" means that faith, vows, and practice (holding the name) are inseparable, are the essential purport of this sutra, and are also the essential path of Pure Land cultivation. "Faith and vows are the practice of wisdom; holding the name is the practice of action," and "the practice of wisdom is the guide, and the practice of action is the primary cultivation, like the eye and foot working together," mean: faith and vows are the guide, like the eye of genuine faith and sincere vows; holding the name is the primary cultivation, like the two feet. Without eyes one wanders blindly, and without feet one cannot advance at all. Therefore, reading from the context of "whether rebirth is attained depends entirely on the presence or absence of faith and vows; the higher or lower grade depends entirely on the depth or shallowness of holding the name,

the meaning of these two lines is: one who attains rebirth must have faith and vows; and moreover must have the practice of holding the name — one whose practice is deep is reborn in a high grade, one whose practice is shallow is reborn in a low grade.

Question: That is not right. The meaning of "whether rebirth is attained depends entirely on the presence or absence of faith and vows" should be: as long as there are faith and vows, rebirth is attained.
Answer: Understood in this way, there are two problems:

First: If understood this way, then the meaning of "whether rebirth is attained depends entirely on the presence or absence of faith and vows; the higher or lower grade depends entirely on the depth or shallowness of holding the name" becomes: as long as there are faith and vows, rebirth is attained; as long as there is the practice of holding the name, rebirth is attained (one whose practice is deep is reborn in a high grade, one whose practice is shallow in a low grade). In this way the first half says that faith and vows alone suffice for rebirth, and the second half says that the practice of holding the name alone suffices for rebirth. So, is rebirth attained through faith and vows alone, or through the practice of holding the name alone? Just consider: how could Master Ouyi utter such a self-contradictory statement!? Therefore, one must take special note of the difference in meaning between the two terms "entirely from" and "entirely by": "entirely from" is a necessary condition, while "entirely by" is a sufficient condition.

Second: In this passage of the Essential Explanation, Master Ouyi is perfectly clear that faith and vows are the guide (leading the path) and holding the name is the primary cultivation (carrying it out). How could it be enough to have only the guide without the primary cultivation? Moreover, the Master gives a vivid simile: faith and vows are like the eye, holding the name like the feet — then for the practitioner to arrive at his destination (the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss), the eyes must look at the road and the feet must walk (eye and foot working together). How could one arrive at the destination with only the eye looking at the road but the feet not walking? Just as Master Ouyi, in the earlier section "Clarifying the Ancestral Doctrine" of the Essential Explanation, teaches: "The ancestral doctrine is the essential path of cultivation

. This sutra takes faith, vows, and holding the name as the essential purport of cultivation. Without faith there is not enough to awaken vows; without vows there is not enough to guide practice; without the wonderful practice of holding the name there is not enough to fulfill the vows and realize the faith.

Faith means believing in oneself and in others, believing in the cause and in the effect, believing in the phenomenal and in the noumenal; vows mean detaching from the Saha world and joyfully seeking the Land of Ultimate Bliss; practice means firmly holding the name,
single-minded and undisturbed
Please note: When Master Ouyi above explained faith, vows, and practice, he clearly states:
"Without the wonderful practice of holding the name, there is not enough to fulfill the vows and realize the faith.
Practice means firmly holding the name, single-minded and undisturbed."
He has thus made entirely clear the relationship among faith, vows, and practice, and the requirement for practice.
The reason reciting the Buddha requires single-mindedness is that
"through the pure mind of reciting the Buddha one moves the causes for rebirth in the Western Pure Land"
— this is the principle of rebirth through reciting the Buddha.
The original words of Master Yinguang's instruction are:

"Only when there is the Pure Land of the mind-only can one be born in the Western Pure Land. If one's own mind is not pure, how can one at once attain rebirth? Even wrongdoers and evil criminals, who gain rebirth through ten sounds of recitation, do so because through the pure mind of reciting the Buddha they move the causes for rebirth in the Western Pure Land."
(Collected Writings of Master Yinguang, "Answering Twenty-Seven Questions of Layman Qu Tianxiang"). Master Yinguang also says:
"Reciting the Buddha with a scattered mind rarely attains rebirth. This method can bring the mind to settle in one place; with single-minded recitation of the Buddha, rebirth is certain."
(Collected Writings of Master Yinguang, "Letter to Layman Chen Xizhou")
Therefore the essential method that ensures rebirth is:
genuine faith, heartfelt vows, single-minded and undisturbed.

This is also the program of study of one who recites the Buddha. Through genuine faith, the eye of wisdom clearly perceives the state before it, seeing the goal and the path distinctly; through heartfelt vows, the power of motivation is incomparably mighty, like a river bursting its banks, sweeping onward with nothing able to withstand it. Having genuine faith and heartfelt vows, one will surely follow the World-Honored One's earnest instruction to practice as taught, and so arrive at the wonderful practice of single-minded undisturbedness; and with this wonderful practice one realizes what one believed and fulfills what one vowed: "Now being single-minded and undisturbed, at the moment of death then
within, one gathers right mindfulness; without, one is welcomed by the Buddha;
laying aside this reward-body, one is actually born in that land." (Master Lianchi, Commentary on the Amitābha Sutra.) Genuine faith and heartfelt vows

What must be noted is that while faith and vows remain merely in the head, they are just an idea. One must put faith and vows into practice; only then are they genuine faith and heartfelt vows. Therefore, genuine faith and heartfelt vows inevitably lead to vigorous practice. Without earnest and diligent recitation of the Buddha, how could one realize what one believes? How could one fulfill what one vows? Faith and vows without vigorous practice are merely empty faith and floating vows. Master Ouyi says:
"The Dharma-gate of reciting the Buddha is nothing special; it only requires deep faith and vigorous practice."
(The Collected Works of Lingfeng)
Therefore, as for the relationship among genuine faith, heartfelt vows, and vigorous practice,
Master Yinguang (the thirteenth Pure Land patriarch)
instructed
saying:

"Since there are genuine faith and heartfelt vows, one should cultivate the primary practice of reciting the Buddha. With faith and vows as the guide, reciting the Buddha is the primary practice. Faith, vows, and practice — these three — are the essential purport of the Dharma-gate of reciting the Buddha.
With practice but no faith and vows, one cannot attain rebirth; with faith and vows but no practice, one likewise cannot attain rebirth.
Faith, vows, and practice complete and lacking nothing, rebirth is certain."
He also says:
"Reciting the Buddha with a scattered mind rarely attains rebirth."
(Collected Writings of Master Yinguang, "Letter to Layman Chen Xizhou")
2. The wonderful method of reciting the Buddha
Chan Master Cao'an says:
"Amitābha Buddha — who cannot recite him, and yet he is especially hard to recite; the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss — who does not wish to be reborn there, and yet few attain it. This is because
(it is because)
the reciters have not obtained the essential method. What is it that makes
(causes)

recitation of the Buddha genuine and true? Is it not this single word "death"! When the word "death" is held before the mind, the states and conditions of the world naturally grow cold, and love and attachment naturally grow light; fame, profit, power, and influence all become of no use here; knowledge, views, and understanding avail nothing at such a time. When the four great elements each disperse, on what will one rely? The lonely ghost without a master, how can it be free? If at this time one does not see Amitābha, one fears one will meet a rakshasa. If one is not reborn in the Pure Land, one fears one will enter a donkey's womb. Even without evil karma, one cannot escape the coming and going of the human realm. Even with wholesome causes, what can one do
(what can be done)
about the heavenly bliss that is so easily exhausted.

Do not say that one has one's own master; driven by the fruits of karma, one truly finds it hard to avoid. Do not say that originally there is no birth and death; while the consciousness-mind is not yet exhausted, it all belongs to the turning of samsara. Do not treat this matter as unhurried; what happens tomorrow, today one does not know. Do not treat this matter lightly; miss this life and one sinks for countless eons. Of all things, none equals the great matter of birth and death; hence all other things are matters of no urgency. At every moment, always make it the moment of death, and then every moment is a time for reciting the Buddha. Reciting in this way is a genuine, heartfelt mind; with such a heartfelt mind, only then is one born in the Pure Land. One must put forth death-determined effort before the Pure Land karma is achieved; one must constantly think of the time of death before one is willing to be single-minded. This is the stairway to Buddhahood, and it is in truth the wonderful essential teaching of reciting the Buddha."
[Rakshasa] the general name for evil ghosts.

[Of all things, none equals the great matter of birth and death, so all other things are matters of no urgency] Nothing is greater than the great matter of birth and death, and so all other things are not urgent matters.
Master Yinguang says:

"People in this world who cannot transcend the ordinary and enter the sage's state, and escape birth and death, are all caused by deluded thoughts. Now when reciting the Buddha, think of oneself as already dead and not yet reborn. In thought after thought, put all the emotional thoughts of the world entirely out of mind; apart from this single phrase of the Buddha's name, there is no thought to be had. How can one bring this about? Because I am already dead, all the deluded thoughts are of no use. If one can recite in this way, there will surely be great benefit."
(Letter in Reply to Layman Zhu Zhonghua, II)
3. A couplet for the Buddha-recitation hall
(Inscribed by Master Yinguang for the Buddha-recitation hall of Kaiyuan Temple in Wuxi)
One should make the vow, the vow to be reborn — let the streams and hills of the traveler's road be loved as they may
Since one does not return, yet upon returning all is attained — who would dispute the wind and moonlight of one's native home?
